body: The light stays off because it wakes his brother, so a young man puts his boots on in the dark, sitting on the edge of a bed in a cold flat at twenty past five on a Wednesday in February. The kettle has not boiled and he has decided not to wait for it. The van has to be loaded by six and the heater does not start working until somewhere around the ninth junction. He has been doing this since October. Nobody knows he does it, in the sense that nobody has ever remarked on it, and the debt it is paying off is not his.

That was courage. It will not be called that by anybody, including him. If you asked him he would say he was just getting on with it, which is the phrase men use for the thing when they are actually doing it.

Courage is sold to young men as a moment. There is a stand to be taken, a room to be walked into, a sentence to be said out loud at cost. Those moments are real and they do arrive. They are also a rounding error in the total.

It is worth taking the word boring literally. Boredom is a technical condition and not merely a mood: the same input arriving again, with no novelty in it, and no feedback to tell you whether any of it is landing. Most of the qualities we admire are easy to summon in the presence of novelty and an audience. Adrenaline is a loan and a crowd is a subsidy. Take both away and what remains has to be paid for out of the man himself, at five in the morning, in February, with nothing arriving to confirm the decision. An idea of manhood built out of the dramatic version leaves a person unprepared for that.

This band was built on the same assumption. The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air right now, playing into rooms with nobody in them and playing exactly the same whether or not a single person has tuned in.

Which costs something. An hour that runs at four in the morning to almost nobody is expensive in the only currency broadcasting has, and there is no way to make that hour look impressive afterwards. It is carried anyway, because the hour is the point. A man is under the same arithmetic. Nobody is ever going to congratulate you for the thing that actually took courage, because nobody is going to know it happened. The visible acts collect the credit; the load is carried on a morning nobody has heard about.

That has become a strange thing to say out loud. A young man now grows up inside an apparatus that treats the unrecorded as very nearly the unreal — the run is not a run until it is logged, the decency is not decency until somebody has been told. That is not vanity so much as what happens when every act has a publishing surface attached and no other kind of surface at all. The effect is a slow redefinition in which courage stops meaning doing the hard thing and starts meaning being seen to have done it.

The dial is arranged to resist that. Every station holds one frequency permanently, no two share a number, and the schedule is published before it airs rather than assembled around whoever happens to be listening. Nothing is rearranged overnight because the figures would look tidier some other way. Learn roughly where things sit and you can find a station without looking, which is precisely the skill a real dial teaches: turning up at a fixed place, repeatedly, and finding that it has held.
There is a competing model of how men are changed, and it is not a stupid one. It deserves to be taken at its best.

The intensity model says that a man is remade by concentrated experience: the weekend away, the thirty-day challenge, the cold water and the early alarm undertaken as a programme with an end date. It works, as far as it goes. Most men come out of one having named something that had been unnameable for years, and the resolve is sincere while it lasts. What the format cannot reach is the fifth month. It has no mechanism for the Wednesday with nothing in it, because the engine of the thing is that this week is not an ordinary week. Anything that runs on being unlike ordinary life will be defeated by ordinary life, which is almost all of the life there is.
Courage is not a burst. It is a rate.

A man of about thirty sits at a kitchen table on a Sunday night and writes a letter to his father, who is in prison and has four years left to serve. The letter is dull on purpose — the weather, the dog, the score, a thing his daughter said about the bins. He buys stamps in books of twelve so there is never a Sunday when he cannot post one. He has been doing this for four years and has had two replies, one of which was a single page. His wife knows. Nobody else does, because there is no way of mentioning it that does not sound like asking for something. He seals it, puts it on top of his keys, and goes to bed.

That is the mechanism, and there is no shorter route to it. Nothing in that sequence produced a feeling worth having on the night. It produced a fortnightly fact that a man in a cell can set a calendar by.

The honest difficulty is that from the inside this is indistinguishable from being stuck. There is no signal that tells a man whether he is enduring something or simply wasting years on it, and the boring kind of courage arrives without the reassurance the dramatic kind gets for nothing. You will be told, sincerely and by people who love you, that you have surely done enough now. Some of the time they will be right, and you will not be able to tell which time this is.

But the absence of confirmation is not a defect in the arrangement. It is the arrangement. A courage that were witnessed would be partly a performance, and the performance is the first part to fall away in the week it becomes expensive. What survives a flat year is whatever was never being done for the room. That is why the unwitnessed version is the harder one, and the only one that can be relied on later, when something serious asks whether you are a man who continues.

So the thing to build is not a reserve of bravery kept for the day it is called for. It is a rate you can hold when nothing is happening: the same hour, the same duty, the same decency shown to the same unnoticing person, long past the point where it produces any feeling. The word the New Testament reaches for far more often than any word for daring is the one usually turned into endurance. That is not an accident of vocabulary. It is a description of what the work mostly consists of.
All of which is theory until it is five in the morning again. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards, 40 frequencies carrying 29 languages. All of it runs to a schedule published before it airs, so none of it is waiting to find out what you are in the mood for.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 309.30 — Gospel Country. Of everything on this dial it is the station made out of the material this article has been about. Country is the one popular form that never stopped writing about the flat year: the job taken for the money, the debt that belonged to somebody else, the man who keeps turning up because he said he would. It is anchored in Nashville, hosted by Elias Inspire, and it runs day and night; the hour at six in the evening is called the Front-Porch Hour, which tells you most of what you need to know about its register. Put it on in the van. It will not inform you that you are doing something extraordinary. It will keep you company while you do it anyway.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually own. Add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for at half past five in the morning — which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not evaluate it and do not explore it; those are words for a man with a free afternoon, and you have a van to load. Put HM 309.30 on tomorrow morning while you are doing the thing nobody is ever going to congratulate you for, and then leave it alone. Give it a month of ordinary Wednesdays. Courage is a rate and so is a radio station, and the only way to find out whether either one is holding is to let it run when nothing at all is happening.
